q: Which tongue landmark marks where the thyroid began?
x: The thyroid bud forms in pharyngeal-floor endoderm at the foramen cecum and descends along the thyroglossal duct; the foramen cecum is the pit left on the tongue when the duct involutes.

w.Circumvallate papillae: These taste papillae form a V just in front of the sulcus terminalis; they mark taste-bud territory served by the glossopharyngeal nerve, not thyroid origin.
w.Lingual tonsil: The lingual tonsil is lymphoid tissue on the posterior tongue; a lingual thyroid can sit nearby, but the tonsil is not the embryologic starting point.
w.Median glossal sulcus: This groove marks where the two lateral lingual swellings fused in the midline of the anterior tongue; the thyroid began farther back.
w.Lingual frenulum: The frenulum is a mucosal fold under the tongue that anchors it to the floor of the mouth; it has no link to thyroid descent.

pt.say: Start at the top of the descent path: the foramen cecum at the tongue base is where the follicular-cell endoderm began its migration.

q: Which embryologic tissue gives rise to thyroid C cells?
x: C cells come from neural crest that migrates into the fourth pharyngeal pouch, forms the ultimobranchial body and fuses with the thyroid; that origin explains why medullary carcinoma secretes calcitonin.

w.Pharyngeal floor endoderm: Pharyngeal floor endoderm forms the follicular cells that make thyroglobulin, T4 and T3; the calcitonin-secreting cells arrive separately.
w.Third pouch endoderm: The third pouch forms the inferior parathyroids and thymus, which descend together; it contributes no cells to the thyroid gland.
w.Second arch mesoderm: Second-arch mesoderm forms the muscles of facial expression and the stapes, supplied by the facial nerve; it forms no endocrine cells.
w.Stomodeal ectoderm: Stomodeal ectoderm forms Rathke's pouch, the origin of the anterior pituitary, not any cell population inside the thyroid.

pt.say: Follow the right panel: neural crest cells reach the fourth pouch and ultimobranchial body, then become parafollicular C cells.

q: Which thyroid structure is the lowest remnant of the thyroglossal duct?
x: The pyramidal lobe projects upward from the isthmus toward the hyoid; it is the lowest segment of the thyroglossal duct that failed to involute, and it is found in many normal people.

w.Isthmus: The isthmus is the normal bridge joining the two lobes across the upper tracheal rings; it is the gland itself, not a duct remnant.
w.Lingual thyroid: A lingual thyroid is tissue that never descended and stays at the tongue base, the top of the duct path rather than its lowest end.
w.Ligament of Berry: Berry's ligament is the posterior suspensory ligament fixing the gland to the cricoid and trachea, which is why the thyroid moves with swallowing.
w.Tubercle of Zuckerkandl: This is a posterior projection of the lateral lobe near the recurrent laryngeal nerve; it is normal lobe tissue, not a duct remnant.

pt.say: Look at the bottom remnant box: the pyramidal lobe marks where the lowest segment of the thyroglossal duct persisted above the isthmus.

q: Which agent blocks iodide uptake at the sodium-iodide symporter?
x: Perchlorate, like pertechnetate, is an anion of similar size and charge to iodide, so it competes for the basolateral sodium-iodide symporter and starves the gland of substrate.

w.Methimazole: Methimazole acts later, inhibiting thyroid peroxidase so iodide already inside the cell is not organified or coupled; trapping continues normally.
w.Propylthiouracil: Propylthiouracil blocks thyroid peroxidase and peripheral 5'-deiodinase; neither action prevents the transporter from concentrating iodide.
w.Lithium: Lithium is concentrated by the gland and inhibits hormone release from thyroglobulin, which is why it causes goiter and hypothyroidism, not an uptake block.
w.Amiodarone: Amiodarone delivers a huge iodine load and inhibits deiodinase; it floods the gland with iodide rather than blocking its entry.

pt.say: Step 1 on the blood side: the sodium-iodide symporter traps iodide, and perchlorate or pertechnetate competes for it.

q: Which enzyme attaches iodine to tyrosines on thyroglobulin?
x: Thyroid peroxidase, on the apical membrane, oxidizes iodide and iodinates tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin to form MIT and DIT, then couples them; thionamides inhibit it.

w.5'-deiodinase: Deiodinase removes iodine rather than adding it, converting T4 into T3 in peripheral tissues after the hormone is secreted.
w.Tyrosine hydroxylase: Tyrosine hydroxylase adds a hydroxyl group to make L-DOPA, the first step of catecholamine synthesis, not iodination.
w.Lysosomal protease: Lysosomal proteases digest thyroglobulin after endocytosis to free finished T4 and T3; iodination happened earlier in the colloid.
w.Iodotyrosine dehalogenase: This enzyme strips iodine from free MIT and DIT released during proteolysis so the gland can recycle it; it removes rather than attaches iodine.

pt.say: In the colloid column, step 2 shows thyroid peroxidase iodinating tyrosines on thyroglobulin, the step methimazole and PTU block.

q: Coupling which two iodotyrosines produces T3?
x: Coupling MIT and DIT gives triiodothyronine, T3, with three iodines, while DIT plus DIT gives T4 with four; thyroid peroxidase performs both couplings on thyroglobulin.

w.DIT and DIT: Two DITs carry four iodines between them, so their coupling makes T4, the main secreted product, not T3.
w.MIT and MIT: Two MITs would carry only two iodines, which forms no active thyroid hormone; MIT is used only in combination with DIT.
w.DIT and reverse T3: Reverse T3 is an inactive peripheral product of inner-ring deiodination of T4; it is never a coupling substrate in the colloid.
w.MIT and tyrosine: Uniodinated tyrosine residues are not coupled; iodination by thyroid peroxidase must come first, making MIT or DIT before any coupling.

pt.say: Look at step 3 in the colloid: coupling MIT and DIT makes T3, while DIT plus DIT makes T4.

q: Which hormone makes up most of the thyroid gland's secretion?
x: About 80 percent of secreted hormone is T4, a prohormone with a long half-life; tissue 5'-deiodinase converts it to T3, which binds the nuclear receptor far more strongly.

w.T3: T3 is the active hormone, but only about 20 percent of it comes straight from the gland; most is made in tissues from T4.
w.Reverse T3: Reverse T3 is an inactive product of inner-ring deiodination in tissues; the gland secretes very little of it.
w.Calcitonin: Calcitonin comes from the parafollicular C cells in small amounts and lowers calcium; it is not a metabolic thyroid hormone.
w.Thyroglobulin: Thyroglobulin is the storage scaffold in the colloid; only traces leak into blood, which is why it serves as a tumor marker after thyroidectomy.

pt.say: Read the blood column: T4 makes up about 80 percent of what the gland releases, and T3 only about 20 percent.

q: What is the brief block of organification after a large iodide load called?
x: The Wolff-Chaikoff effect is autoregulation: a large iodide load transiently inhibits organification, protecting against hormone excess; a normal gland escapes in days, but a damaged gland can become hypothyroid.

w.Jod-Basedow phenomenon: Jod-Basedow is the opposite outcome: iodine given to a deficient patient with autonomous nodules increases synthesis and causes thyrotoxicosis.
w.Sick euthyroid syndrome: Sick euthyroid syndrome is reduced peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 during severe illness, with high reverse T3, not an organification block.
w.Hashitoxicosis: Hashitoxicosis is the transient thyrotoxic leak of stored hormone early in Hashimoto thyroiditis, caused by follicle destruction rather than iodide.
w.Hook effect: The hook effect is an immunoassay artifact in which huge antigen levels give a falsely low result, as with giant prolactinomas; it is not physiology.

pt.say: In the colloid column, the Wolff-Chaikoff line marks how iodide excess briefly halts organification by thyroid peroxidase.

q: Iodinated contrast makes a patient with an iodine-deficient nodular goiter thyrotoxic. What is this called?
x: In the Jod-Basedow phenomenon, autonomous nodules that were substrate-limited by iodine deficiency convert the new iodine into excess hormone, because they do not respond to TSH suppression.

w.Wolff-Chaikoff effect: The Wolff-Chaikoff effect is a transient shutdown of organification after iodide excess, which tends toward hypothyroidism rather than thyrotoxicosis.
w.Hashitoxicosis: Hashitoxicosis is a brief leak of stored hormone from autoimmune follicle destruction; it is not triggered by an iodine load on nodules.
w.Thyroid storm: Thyroid storm is life-threatening decompensated thyrotoxicosis with fever and delirium; contrast can precipitate it, but iodine-fueled nodular overproduction has its own name.
w.de Quervain thyroiditis: De Quervain thyroiditis follows a viral illness and causes a painful, tender gland with a high ESR and low uptake, not iodine-driven synthesis.

pt.say: In the high-uptake panel, the toxic multinodular goiter holds autonomous nodules; given iodine, they produce the Jod-Basedow phenomenon.

q: Thyroid hormone raises heart rate chiefly by increasing which receptor?
x: T3 increases transcription of cardiac beta-1 adrenergic receptors, so normal catecholamine levels produce more tachycardia and contractility; that is why beta-blockers relieve thyrotoxic symptoms quickly.

w.Alpha-1 adrenergic receptor: Alpha-1 receptors constrict vascular smooth muscle; thyrotoxicosis actually lowers systemic vascular resistance, and alpha-1 activity does not set heart rate.
w.M2 muscarinic receptor: M2 receptors carry vagal slowing of the sinoatrial node; more M2 signaling would lower heart rate, the opposite of thyrotoxic tachycardia.
w.Beta-2 adrenergic receptor: Beta-2 receptors relax bronchial and vascular smooth muscle; they contribute little to sinus rate, which is driven by cardiac beta-1 receptors.
w.Dopamine D1 receptor: D1 receptors dilate renal and splanchnic vessels; thyroid hormone does not raise heart rate through dopaminergic signaling.

pt.say: Look at the tissue band: T3 on its nuclear receptor induces beta-1 receptors, which raises heart rate and contractility.

q: Which lab pattern indicates central hypothyroidism?
o: Low free T4, normal or low TSH
x: In central hypothyroidism the pituitary or hypothalamus fails, so TSH cannot rise as free T4 falls; it stays low or inappropriately normal, and screening by TSH alone misses it.

w.Low free T4, high TSH: A high TSH with low free T4 means the gland itself is failing, as in Hashimoto thyroiditis, while the pituitary responds normally.
w.Normal free T4, high TSH: This is subclinical hypothyroidism: early gland failure in which TSH rises first to hold free T4 in range.
w.High free T4, low TSH: An autonomous or stimulated gland, as in Graves disease, suppresses TSH through feedback; this is primary hyperthyroidism.
w.Normal free T4, low TSH: This is subclinical hyperthyroidism, or T3 toxicosis if T3 is high; hCG in the first trimester can also produce it.

pt.say: Find the low free T4 column: central hypothyroidism sits where TSH is inappropriately normal or low, because the pituitary cannot respond.

q: Which drug raises total T4 while leaving free T4 normal?
x: Oral estrogen increases hepatic synthesis of thyroxine-binding globulin, so more T4 is bound; the gland makes extra until free T4 and TSH are normal again, leaving only total T4 high.

w.Testosterone: Androgens lower thyroxine-binding globulin, so total T4 falls, not rises, while free T4 and TSH stay normal.
w.Prednisone: Glucocorticoids lower binding globulin and inhibit 5'-deiodinase, so total T4 tends to fall and T3 drops; they do not raise total T4.
w.Methimazole: Methimazole blocks thyroid peroxidase, reducing synthesis of both total and free T4 rather than changing binding proteins.
w.Lithium: Lithium inhibits release of hormone from the gland and can cause hypothyroidism with a high TSH; it lowers free and total T4.

pt.say: In the center box the patient is euthyroid; oral estrogen raises binding globulin, which moves total T4 but not free T4.

q: Which finding marks sick euthyroid syndrome?
x: Severe illness inhibits 5'-deiodinase, so T3 falls while inner-ring deiodination makes more reverse T3, which is also cleared slowly; TSH and free T4 stay near normal, and no treatment is needed.

w.High TSH: A high TSH signals primary hypothyroidism; in sick euthyroid syndrome TSH is normal or low, sometimes briefly rising during recovery.
w.High free T4: High free T4 with suppressed TSH marks thyrotoxicosis; critical illness leaves free T4 normal or slightly low.
w.Positive anti-TPO antibodies: Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies mark autoimmune thyroid disease such as Hashimoto thyroiditis, an intrinsic gland problem unrelated to illness.
w.High thyroglobulin: Thyroglobulin rises when follicles are destroyed or stimulated, as in thyroiditis or Graves disease, not with reduced peripheral deiodination.

pt.say: Look at the low TSH, low free T4 corner: severe illness gives low T3 with high reverse T3, the sick euthyroid pattern.

q: Which follicle appearance shows active stimulation by TSH or Graves antibodies?
x: Stimulation makes follicular cells tall and columnar, and rapid endocytosis leaves scalloped, pale colloid at the cell edge; a resting follicle has flatter cells and abundant stored colloid.

w.Flat cells, abundant dense colloid: Flat cells full of stored colloid are a resting or suppressed follicle, as when TSH is low, the opposite of active stimulation.
w.Lymphoid follicles with germinal centers: Germinal centers and Hurthle cells define Hashimoto thyroiditis, an autoimmune destruction that eventually lowers hormone output.
w.Granulomas with multinucleated giant cel: Granulomas with giant cells mark subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis, a painful, destructive process after a viral illness.
w.Dense fibrosis replacing follicles: Fibrosis extending beyond the capsule is Riedel thyroiditis, a hard, fixed gland that is usually euthyroid or hypothyroid.

pt.say: In the follicular-cell box, Graves antibodies produce tall cells with scalloped colloid, the look of a gland that is actively stimulated.
